title: CPU engine with libomp (2 threads)
hypothesis: The installed engine was single-threaded; libomp should let it use more cores.
conclusion: Measured 0.10 tok/s, but Colibri only used 2 threads on the M6 (see threads). Reference point for the GPU steps.

title: Metal GPU backend
hypothesis: Expert math and attention were on the CPU; the GPU was idle.
conclusion: Expert math and attention moved to the GPU; the SSD became the largest cost.

title: Overlap SSD reads with GPU work
hypothesis: Reads and math happen one after the other; overlapping should hide some read time.
conclusion: Small gain within noise on its own; kept because it combines with DIRECT.

title: Uncached SSD reads
hypothesis: Reading around the page cache avoids a copy and enables zero-copy GPU buffers.
conclusion: Faster; Colibri reports DIRECT can be drive-dependent.

title: Metal residency set
hypothesis: Registering resident buffers once should cut per-dispatch GPU scheduling overhead.
conclusion: Attention time fell sharply; GPU scheduling overhead mostly gone.

title: GPU keep-alive spin
hypothesis: A spinning GPU keep-alive should reduce dispatch latency.
conclusion: Faster.
tradeoffs: Uses more power; drop on battery.

title: Best exact combination
hypothesis: The residency set and the spin target different overheads, so they should add up.
conclusion: 0.43-0.44 tok/s, identical text, about 76% of time now waiting on the SSD.

title: 4 SSD readers instead of 8
hypothesis: Fewer readers might reduce contention.
conclusion: Within noise of 8 readers; the SSD is the limit, not the reader count.

title: 2 SSD readers
hypothesis: iobench saturates at 2 readers.
conclusion: No change.

title: 16 SSD readers
hypothesis: More queue depth might help the SSD.
conclusion: No change.

title: Cross-layer expert prefetch
hypothesis: Loading the next layer's likely experts early should hide read time.
conclusion: Hit rate rose to 10% but speed did not; most prefetched loads were discarded.

title: Page cache as the expert cache
hypothesis: Letting macOS cache experts might use free RAM better than slabs.
conclusion: GPU out-of-memory errors on every block; stopped.

title: Expert cache not wired into RAM
hypothesis: Wiring may not matter with a tiny cache.
conclusion: Refused to start: free RAM had dropped to 12.2 GB right after the mmap failure. Inconclusive; retry on a quiet machine.

title: 2 cache slots per layer (RAM 20 GB)
hypothesis: Doubling the expert cache should raise the hit rate.
conclusion: Hit rate 2% to 4%; too small to matter. A useful cache needs tens of GB.

title: CPU-only: 6 threads instead of 2
hypothesis: Colibri uses only the M6's 2 "Super" cores (colibri#2194).
conclusion: CPU math and prompt reading scale with cores.

title: CPU-only: 12 threads instead of 2
hypothesis: Colibri uses only the M6's 2 "Super" cores (colibri#2194).
conclusion: CPU math and prompt reading scale with cores.
tradeoffs: Efficiency cores add heat; 6 vs 12 differences are small.

title: Metal exact: 6 threads instead of 2
hypothesis: Colibri uses only the M6's 2 "Super" cores (colibri#2194).
conclusion: No change: exact Metal runs wait on the SSD.

hypothesis: Prompt reading runs attention on the CPU; the GPU should be faster. Not bit-exact by design.
conclusion: Prompt reading time unchanged (23.5 s vs 23.2 s): it is bound by expert reads, not attention. Generation was 16% slower in this single run, but the code-prompt run saw no change, so treat that as noise or as an effect on draft-verify steps. Not worth using.

title: Skip below 0.30 with 12 threads
hypothesis: Lossy runs spend more time on CPU-side work, which more threads should cut.
conclusion: Same speed as 2 threads (the run is still SSD-bound). Marked the usable everyday setting by the owner on 2026-10-18: quality bench v1 found no real mistakes at skip 0.3 (normal style: 23 correct, 1 cut off by the token cap; terse: 24/24), about 2x exact generation speed, and with terse prompts ~52 s per answer vs ~64 s exact.

title: Skip below 0.40 with 12 threads

title: Skip below 0.50 with 12 threads
hypothesis: Lossy runs spend more time on CPU-side work, which more threads should cut.

title: Second SSD for expert reads
hypothesis: Exact runs are SSD-bound; splitting reads across two drives could nearly double read speed.
conclusion: Not run: needs an external NVMe drive.

title: Lossless compressed experts (int4-rans256-g0)
hypothesis: ~24% fewer bytes to read with byte-exact output.
conclusion: Not run: Colibri has the codec but no engine loader yet; CPU decoding would likely cost what it saves.

title: REAP expert pruning
hypothesis: A smaller model raises the cache hit rate.
conclusion: Not run: still 8 experts per token, so bytes per token stay the same; community GLM cards report quality loss at 34%.

title: 3-bit or mixed-precision experts
hypothesis: int3 cuts expert bytes ~25%.
conclusion: Not run: lossy and needs re-converting 409 GB; papers report large losses at 2-bit.

title: Terse prompting ("answer as briefly as possible")
change: prompt suffix: " Answer as briefly as possible. For code, reply with only the code."
hypothesis: Shorter answers finish sooner even at the same tok/s, if accuracy holds.
conclusion: Quality bench v1 (24 graded prompts): exact answers took 64 s on average instead of 281 s (4.4x faster), with ~10 instead of ~98 output tokens. Every config scored 24/24 terse; normal style had 2 genuinely wrong answers at skip 0.5 (see review). Prompt reading (~40 s) is now most of a terse answer's time.
tradeoffs: Answers are short; ask for detail when needed. Generation speed (tok/s) is unchanged: the gain is fewer tokens.

title: Prompt-lookup drafts off (COLI_LOOKUP=0)
hypothesis: Colibri drafts n-grams from the prompt by default (our runs show 1.04 tokens per forward). Each verify reads experts for every drafted row, so on an SSD-bound run a rejected draft costs a full extra set of expert reads; turning it off could be faster, or show the gate already pays for itself (code prompt repeats more n-grams).
conclusion: 0.40 tok/s vs 0.44 reference (-9%), prompt read 24.7 s. Prompt-lookup drafts neither help nor hurt exact decoding on the sky prompt. Single run on the everyday (busy) Mac during the quiet-run campaign; differences under ~10% are noise.

title: int8 MTP draft head for GLM-5.3
hypothesis: Our glm-5.3 container has no MTP head ("MTP absent"). Colibri reports 2.2-2.8 tokens per forward when it pays. On an SSD-bound run a 3-row verify reads more experts (2% hits), so exact-mode gain is uncertain; output stays identical (only verified tokens are kept).
conclusion: 0.42 tok/s vs 0.44 without the head. The int8 MTP draft head did not speed up exact decoding: drafted tokens still need every expert of the verify pass, so SSD reads stay the limit (io 78% of time). The quality bench (glm-5.3-mtp) matched int4 within noise. Single run on the everyday (busy) Mac during the quiet-run campaign; differences under ~10% are noise.
tradeoffs: ~10 GB more on disk; the head's dense part stays resident (its experts stream like the others), so some RAM leaves the expert cache.

title: GLM-5.3 as a 2-bit GGUF (Unsloth UD-IQ2_M, 239 GB)
change: Colibri dev 16239caa + unsloth GLM-5.3 UD-IQ2_M GGUF (imported)
hypothesis: The 2-bit GGUF is ~239 GB against ~419 GB for the int4 container, so roughly 40% fewer expert bytes per token (~7 GB instead of 12.7 GB): exact-mode SSD ceiling ~0.9 tok/s instead of ~0.5, and lossy skip runs read less too. Risk: Colibri computes GGUF blocks (QT_GGML) on the CPU only, with no Metal copy, so the math may eat the I/O saving; NEON kernels exist. The GGUF carries the MTP (nextn) layer, which Colibri dev turns on.
conclusion: 0.35 tok/s vs 0.44 int4 (-20%) although the files are 43% smaller. SSD share drops to 37%, but attention (32%) and expert math (20%) on the dev engine take over. Quality bench: 23/24 normal, 24/24 terse at exact, within noise of int4. Single run on the everyday (busy) Mac during the quiet-run campaign; differences under ~10% are noise.
tradeoffs: Lossy (2-bit experts); CPU-only expert math for GGUF blocks; a second 239 GB model on disk.

title: Check the Qwen models' architecture (dense vs MoE)
change: read config.json of Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
hypothesis: Artificial Analysis lists Qwen3.8-27B as 3B active, Colibri says dense; expert streaming only helps a MoE.
conclusion: Read from the official config.json files. Qwen3.8-27B is dense: Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration, 64 layers, hidden 5120, one MLP per layer (intermediate 17408), no experts, so all ~27.8B weights are used for every token (Ollama: 27.8B, NVFP4). Artificial Analysis's "3B active" for it is wrong. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is a MoE: Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration, 40 layers, hidden 2048, 256 experts with 8 routed plus 1 shared per token (expert width 512). Routed experts per token are ~1.0B parameters (~0.55 GB at int4 gs64), so expert streaming applies to it and not to the 27B.

title: Qwen3.8-27B (dense) through the installed Ollama MLX model
change: Ollama qwen3.8:27b-mlx fully in RAM; quality bench (normal, terse) in two settings: exact (thinking off, temperature 0, 128 tokens, comparable with GLM) and native (Ollama defaults: thinking on, model sampling, up to 4096 tokens)
hypothesis: Published intelligence 34 vs GLM-5.3 45, but it fits in RAM: likely tens of tok/s, so far more correct answers per minute.
conclusion: Done: 96 answers, published as bench qwen38-27b-ollama. Terse with thinking off: 24/24 correct at 15.9 tok/s, 0.5 s median answer. Native (thinking on): 24/24 normal at 24.7 tok/s (5.8 s median), 23/24 terse. Normal with thinking off and 128 tokens: 18/24, 10 answers cut off. On this 24-question bench it matches GLM-5.3 int4 (24/24 terse) about 30x faster, and Gemma 4 26B / E4B match it faster still; the bench is too easy to show the intelligence gap (published 45 vs 34). Busy machine, single runs.

title: OLMoE: quality on our bench, and total tok/s serving 1, 4 and 10 requests at once
change: One OLMoE-1B-7B 4-bit copy (models/olmoe-1b-7b-4bit, MLX, ~4 GB in memory) behind mlx_lm.server; 24-question bench in both styles; then 1, 4 and 10 concurrent requests
hypothesis: Resident OLMoE decodes ~199 tok/s for one request. Decoding is memory-bound, so one copy serving a batch should give far more total tokens per second than one request, with each request somewhat slower: e.g. 10 parallel answers at several hundred tok/s in total. Running 10 separate copies would cost ~10x the memory (~46 GB peak, more than this Mac has) for no gain. The open question is quality: OLMoE (1B active) is far weaker than the models benched so far, so its correct-answer rate decides whether the throughput is useful.
conclusion: Planned: needs the two harness pieces listed under plan_outline before it can run unattended.
tradeoffs: Batching raises total throughput but slows each answer and raises peak memory (KV cache per request); single-request latency must be reported next to total tok/s.
